10040216:
Wednesday, March 26, 2025
TESTIMONY FROM ANTHONY LYONS
LD 1092 AN ACT TO ENSURE THAT DUAL DISTRIBUTION PROHIBITIONS ARE NOT VIOLATED BY DIRECT SHIPPERS OF WINE
Good Morning,
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee,
My name is Tony Lyons and I am a resident of Auburn, here today representing the Maine Winery Guild and owner of WillowsAwake Winery in Leeds, Maine. Our 67-acre parcel of land is home to WillowsAwake Winery supported by eight acres of vineyard, a state of art winery facility, a tasting room and the No.10 Eatery@WillowsAwake Winery, a Class A Restaurant. Our restaurant operates year-round.
I appreciate the opportunity to offer comments in opposition to the present version of LD 1092, An Act to Ensure That Dual Distribution Prohibitions Are Not Violated by Direct Shippers of Wine.
This bill, in its present form, would prohibit a winery from both being a Direct Shipper AND sell to a wholesale distributor; one or the other. The Guild does not believe that the intent of this bill was to take away current flexibility that Maine wineries have to sell and market their products within Maine.
Currently for a winery in Maine to ship within the State, the winery needs to obtain a Direct Shipper of Wine license from the Bureau of Alcoholic Beverages and Lottey Operations (BABLO). (Title 28-A �1403-A.2. Direct Shipment of Wine) WillowsAwake holds a Direct Shippers License # DSW-23-106932, that allows us to ship our wine within Maine and to other states that allow the direct shipment of wine. This allows us to sell and ship to our tasting room guests who may be travelling and also our Wine Club members.
Additionally, under Title 28-A Chapter 51 �1355-A. Manufacturer licenses 4. B. (1) a licensed winery "may sell or deliver its products to licensed retailers or wholesalers".
So, under current law wineries can both hold a Direct Shippers License and sell through a wholesaler distributor.
WillowsAwake sells specific wines through a Maine wholesale distributor that allows us to have our product available and visible in one of Maine's largest grocery store chains. We have other wines that we sell directly to retailers, ship or self-distribute.

Now the nitty gritty is that when I wish to market a new wine, I need to have the label approved by the federal Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB). Then I can go to the BABLO BELLS system and register that label within the State of Maine. (Following Title 28-A. Approval and Registration of Labels. �6-A.) Within BELLS I can only assign that wine label to either "self-distribute" (under 28-A Chap. 51 �1355-A.4.B (1)) or to a wholesale distributor and its corresponding territory. I cannot currently do both, distribute or sell that label myself AND use a wholesale distributor to sell for me.
In reality then, current law has provisions to achieve what is possibly the intent of this bill but at the wine label level rather than at a more comprehensive prohibition that affects all wine produced by a licensed winery.
The industry in Maine is still relatively small and we need to have flexible opportunities to market our products and gain visibility. The larger Maine wineries have some of their products currently marketed through Maine's wholesale distributors; under this bill, as currently written, they would have to surrender their Direct Shippers Licenses and so be unable to ship any wine to tasting room customers and wine club members, even though currently being in compliance with current statutes.
Again, we do not believe this was the intent of this legislation and we are ready and willing to work with the Committee and the Distributors Association to craft an amendment that fulfills their goal without hurting Maine wineries.
Thank you for your time and I welcome any questions you may have at this time.
10041521:
Bob Craft Orono IGA LD 1092
I, Bob Craft Owner of Orono IGA would like to give support to LD 1092. In this business climate, we are already at many disadvantages trying to build our business and retain customers. It is unfair that a customer can order wine out of state instead of buying locally. How can the company that sells out of state assure that the customer is of age? Does UPS or Fedex get trained to verify age? Can they tell the difference of a fake ID? How is this fair for redemption centers? If Maine cares about its small businesses, then they will not allow out of state companies to take that business away from us. Nothing about letting consumers purchase wine from out of state is good for any of us. These direct shippers are taking money right out of our pockets.
10039204:
March 26, 2025
Senator Craig Hickman - Chair Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee
Representative Laura Supica - Chair Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee
Members of the Joint Standing Committee of Veterans and Legal Affairs
My name is Carrie Rand-Anastasiades, and I am the Director of Northeast States for Wine Institute. Thank you for allowing me to testify today. Wine Institute is a public policy association of over 1,000 California wineries and affiliated suppliers dedicated to advocating for the responsible consumption and enjoyment of wine. We stand in opposition to LD 1092 An Act to Ensure That Dual Distribution Prohibitions Are Not Violated By Direct Shippers, which, if enacted, would prohibit wineries from shipping direct to consumers, if they also do business with a wholesaler in the State of Maine.
Residents of Maine have enjoyed the privilege of being able to order wine and have it shipped to them since 2009. Currently, 45 States allow direct to consumer (DTC) shipping and only 1 State in the nation has a provision like the one proposed in LD 1092. In 2023, Maine consumers purchased 1,618,671 nine-liter cases of wine. Only 21,696 of those cases were cases of wine shipped directly to consumers. Translated, this means that 98.66% of wine was sold and distributed through the three-tier system, and only 1.34% was sold via the DTC channel in the State.
Many people order more high-end wine via DTC that is not available through the wholesale/retail channel but also enjoy the convenience of purchasing vintages that are also sold through those means. Allowing both to be sold through the three-tiered system and DTC further strengthens the brand and makes a customer more apt to reach for it when they are purchasing at retail. The wholesale channel is also not fool proof, as much depends on what the individual retail store is purchasing in response to their customer base. If the store in Denmark, ME does not order a specific brand or vintage from the wholesaler, the customer does not have easy access to it, even though

the label is being distributed to stores in Kennebunkport. Direct shipment makes this possible. Consumers can order many vintages in limited amounts (12 cases per year) for personal consumption, according to their personal palate. They also do this at a higher cost as they pay shipping and handling charges. Passage of this bill would take that choice away from residents.
Effective July 1st all DTC shipments will be included in the Maine Bottle deposit system. Wineries are already registering with comingling cooperatives to ensure pick up and proper recycling of the products. In addition, we have worked hard to establish registration of fulfillment houses and reporting from carriers that ship our wines. We want to make sure that the process is completely transparent, and that the product is not falling into the wrong hands.
With the rise of inflationary pressures reducing household spending, cannabis products as alternatives to alcohol, and cultural wellness trends leading to reduced alcohol consumption, sales for 2024 were down 10%. Prohibiting wineries from selling direct to consumers if they also do business with a wholesaler will only further decrease tax and permit revenue received by the State. But more importantly, prohibiting these sales will rob consumers of choices that they are currently enjoying, and take Maine out of line with the policy 44 other states implement. It is because of this that we ask you to preserve the right to sell our product via wholesalers as well as direct to consumers, by voting against LD 1092.

MBDA
Maine Beverage Distributors Association

March 26, 2025
LD 1092, An Act to Ensure that Dual Distribution Prohibitions Are Not Violated by Direct Shippers of Wine
Good morning, Sen. Hickman, Rep. Supica and members of the VLA committee. I am Cheryl Timberlake, a resident ofMt. Vernon. I serve as the Executive Vice President of the Maine Beverage Distributors Association (MBDA). As family-owned businesses who have been in operation since Prohibition, MBDA remains committed to championing a smartly regulated alcohol distribution system where suppliers, wholesalers, and retailers maintain their distinct roles and independence. MBDA is in strong support ofLD 1092.
I want to thank the sponsors Rep. Chapman, Boy er and Hymes. As noted in the opening remarks, this bill remedies a conflict in statute regarding the direct sale by a winery to a Maine consumer in a territory exclusively assigned to a Maine distributor
Maine Revised Statute Section 1403-A permits Certificate of Approval Holders (COA) to directly ship wine to Maine consumers subject to certain limitations.
Title 28-A Chapter 57 provides specific licensing requirements for wine wholesalers and COAs. Section 1453 which prohibits dual distribution.
When a winery enters a relationship with a Maine wholesaler, they execute a distribution agreement, which includes designation of a sales territory and the list of products the wholesaler is authorized to distribute. All distribution agreements embody exclusive territory assignments. The winery, COA, files the application with BABLO.
If a "direct shipper" sells wine to a consumer located in a territory assigned to a Maine wine distributor, that sale would violate the prohibition on dual distribution provided in Maine Revised Statutes � 1453.
MBDA is concerned that wineries may sell into a distributor's territory and thereby violate � 1453 and breach their distribution agreements.

To avoid violation of the dual distribution statute and the exclusive territory provision in distribution agreements, this bill will restrict the wine direct shipper permit to those wineries that have not entered into a distribution agreement with any Maine wine distributors.
Distributors build wine brands, invest in their inventory, provide retailer education and expertise. MBDA wants to ensure accounts have the portfolio of products to their customers' desire. Our members service over 1000 retail wine accounts throughout the state. These licensees provide more than 12,000 unique wine SKUs for customers.
The attached list ofDTC permits represents the last 60 days of license renewal/activity. There are several large manufacturers identified which have distributor representation. What is unlcnown from this report is whether these wineries have a DTC permit for wine varieties distinct from those wines included in the distribution agreement.
This issue was brought to our attention by a local winery who has a DTC permit and an assigned distributor. During our discussion we came to understand that the permit process may differentiate the label declarations as to how the wine DTC shipper intends to sell the wine, self- distribution or distributor assignment.
This is a distinction that is not clarified in the current bill draft.
Thank you for your consideration of our comments. I would be happy to answer any questions now or during the work session.

WINE DUAL DISTRIBUTION ANALYSIS:
A winery which does not have an exclusive distribution agreement with a Maine distributor can ship directly to a Maine consumer with a permit. But a winery which already has an exclusive distribution agreement with a Maine distributor does not need the privilege of selling direct to a consumer, nor does a JVIaine consumer within such territory need to be able to purchase direct from the winery because the wine is available through local retailers.
If a "direct shipper" sells wine to a consumer located in a territory assigned to a Maine wine distributor, that sale would violate the prohibition on dual distribution embodied in IVIaine Revised Statute � 1453.
The direct sale by a winery to a IVIaine consumer in a territoiy exclusively assigned to a Mmne distributor would constitute a breach of the distribution agreement.

10041524:
David Pike Orono LD 1092
I, David Pike Owner of Orono IGA would like to give support to LD 1092. In this business climate, we are already at many disadvantages trying to build our business and retain customers. It is unfair that a customer can order wine out of state instead of buying locally. How can the company that sells out of state assure that the customer is of age? Does UPS or Fedex get trained to verify age? Can they tell the difference of a fake ID? How is this fair for redemption centers? If Maine cares about its small businesses, then they will not allow out of state companies to take that business away from us. Nothing about letting consumers purchase wine from out of state is good for any of us. These direct shippers are taking money right out of our pockets.
10039757:
JANET T. MILLS GOVERNOR

STATE OF MAINE DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES BUREAU OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES AND LOTTERY OPERATIONS

8 STATE HOUSE STATION AUGUSTA, MAINE 04333-0008

KIRSTEN LC FIGUEROA COMMISSIONER
LOUIS J. LUCHINI DIRECTOR

March 26, 2025
Testimony of the Bureau of Alcoholic Beverages and Lottery Operations Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs
Neither For Nor Against LD 1092 An Act to Ensure That Dual Distribution Prohibitions Are Not Violated by Direct Shippers of Wine
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs: I am Louis Luchini and I'm the Director of the Bureau of Alcoholic Beverages and Lottery Operations. We are here to testify neither for nor against LD 1092, An Act to Ensure That Dual Distribution Prohibitions Are Not Violated by Direct Shippers of Wine, but wish to provide additional information for the committee's consideration.
Background
Fifteen years ago, the 124th Legislature passed legislation authorizing the direct shipment of wine to consumers. Maine is now one of approximately 45 states that allow for direct shipping of wine, with varying levels of regulation. Under 28-A MRS 1403-A, a small winery or winery that holds a state license and federal basic wine manufacturing permit may apply for a direct shipper license with the Bureau. Shipments must be made by a common carrier.
During the 131st Legislature, the Bureau introduced LD 2148, which sought to improve direct shipper and common carrier reporting to ensure compliance with direct shipping laws.
Direct Shipping is not dual distribution
Related to the title of this bill - the direct shipment of wine does not violate Maine law prohibiting dual distribution. We believe the law is clear, as was the Legislature's intent in allowing direct shipping of wine in the manner that it has been conducted for the last 15 years.
Impacts of LD 1092
We encourage the committee to consider the impacts of this legislation, which are significant. This bill proposes to prohibit any winery or small winery from direct shipping if they have an agreement with a wholesale licensee in Maine (wineries also include hard cideries and meaderies). In real numbers, we estimate that there are approximately 190 wineries/small wineries that currently hold a direct shipper license that would no longer be eligible should this bill become law.
Thank you for your time. I will be available for the work session at the committee's request.
187499:
Wednesday, March 26, 2025
TESTIMONY FROM ANTHONY LYONS LD 1092 AN ACT TO ENSURE THAT DUAL DISTRIBUTION PROHIBITIONS ARE NOT
VIOLATED BY DIRECT SHIPPERS OF WINE
Good Morning,
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and members of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee,
My name is Tony Lyons and I am a resident of Auburn, here today representing the Maine Winery Guild and owner of WillowsAwake Winery in Leeds, Maine. Our 67-acre parcel of land is home to WitlowsAwake Winery supported by eight acres of vineyard, a state of art winery facility, a tasting room and the No.10 Eatery@WillowsAwake Winery, a Class A Restaurant. Our restaurant operates year-round.
I appreciate the opportunity to offer comments in opposition to the present version of LD 1092, An Act to Ensure That Dual Distribution Prohibitions Are Not Violated by Direct Shippers of Wine.
This bill, in its present form, would prohibit a winery from both being a Direct Shipper AND sell to a wholesale distributor; one or the other. The Guild does not believe that the intent of this bill was to take away current flexibility that Maine wineries have to sell and market their products within Maine.
Currently for a winery in Maine to ship within the State, the winery needs to obtain a Direct Shipper of Wine license from the Bureau of Alcoholic Beverages and Lottey Operations (BABLO). (Title 28-A S1403-A.2. Direct Shipment of Wine) WillowsAwake holds a Direct Shippers License # DSW-23-106932, that allows us to ship our wine within Maine and to other states that allow the direct shipment of wine. This allows us to sell and ship to our tasting room guests who may be travelling and also our Wine Club members.
Additionally, under Title 28-A Chapter 51 S1355-A. Manufacturer licenses 4. B. (1) a licensed winery "may sell or deliver its products to licensed retailers or wholesalers".
So, under current law wineries can both hold a Direct Shippers License and sell through a wholesaler distributor.
WillowsAwake sells specific wines through a Maine wholesale distributor that allows us to have our product available and visible in one of Maine's largest grocery store chains. We have other wines that we sell directly to retailers, ship or self-distribute.

Now the nitty gritty is that when I wish to market a new wine, I need to have the label approved by the federal Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB). Then I can go to the BABLO BELLS system and register that label within the State of Maine. (Following Title 28'A. Approval and Registration of Labels. S6-A.) Within BELLS I can only assign that wine label to either "self-distribute" (under 28-A Chap. 51 S1355-A.4.B (1)) or to a wholesale distributor and its corresponding territory. I cannot currently do both, distribute or sell that label myself AND use a wholesale distributor to sell for me.
In reality then, current law has provisions to achieve what is possibly the intent of this bill but at the wine label level rather than at a more comprehensive prohibition that affects alt wine produced by a licensed winery.
The industry in Maine is still relatively small and we need to have flexible opportunities to market our products and gain visibility. The larger Maine wineries have some of their products currently marketed through Maine's wholesale distributors; under this bill, as currently written, they would have to surrender their Direct Shippers Licenses and so be unable to ship any wine to tasting room customers and wine club members, even though currently being in compliance with current statutes.
Again, we do not believe this was the intent of this legislation and we are ready and willing to work with the Committee and the Distributors Association to craft an amendment that fulfills their goal without hurting Maine wineries.
Thank you for your time and I welcome any questions you may have at this time.
